hook: A gentle, funny entry: a house in Queensland where someone from another world writes messages in the condensation on the windows, and the Foundation's answer is to move a doctor in to write back. It is short and almost all dialogue. The one thing to know going in is that the doctor is not entirely honest with his new pen pal about what he is.
whyItMatters: The article is a satire of racism told from the other side of the glass. Beauremont, a tentacled being with a brown carapace, talks about humans in the exact stock phrases of real-world bigotry and anti-immigrant talk, so the joke lands because every line is one you have heard before with a different group swapped in. The comedy tag fits, but the target is pointed and specific.
thingsToNotice: Beauremont runs through the whole script: it is not racist, some of its best friends are human, humans are taking its jobs and cost it a promotion, violence would just be the natural result, and surely nobody wants a spawnsib marrying one. The doctor survives by simply agreeing and claiming to look the same as it, seven tendrils tall. The punchline is the agent who introduces himself as a human: Beauremont is effusively polite to his face, then tells the doctor it put that lippy gamete in his place. Containment here amounts to keeping a fake identity and a friendly correspondence going, and the hand-drawn smiley face with its oddly placed dots is a small, nice detail.
